title: Transparency, Unanimity & Diversity -- Ch. 5: Excellence Is Not Enough
keywords: Time magazine Person of the Century
the Internet and the dotcom mania
the Ten Commandments and the Beatitudes
accountability and transparency in public service
primary_topics: Chapter 5 of 'Transparency, Unanimity & Diversity' -- CJP's address to the Phi Kappa Phi Honor Society and the Civil Service Commission round table, whose thesis is that while the conference rightly prized 'Excellence in Government Service,' excellence is not enough: it must be joined by ethics and eternity, and, for public servants, by transparency.

His experiential account of the e-society -- reading Manila dailies on the Internet from New York hours before Philippine readers, the single Disney card that unlocked a resort larger than Makati, text messaging across 2,000 kilometers of Turkey, and Encarta replacing shelves of encyclopedias -- set against a country still mired in poverty, rebellion, corruption and criminality.

His treatment of excellence as a duty to develop to the maximum whatever gift one was given, argued through the contrasting career paths of his only son (seventeen years of study, then straight into a vice presidency at Bear Stearns) and his own (short schooling, then climbing from a lowly associate to the Supreme Court), and through Learned Hand's ideal magistrate steeped in the humanities.

His distinction between ethical values and image-building tactics, his call for 'a change in men' rather than a change of men, his account of spiritual laws and eternity, and his closing equation GG=TE3 -- good governance equals transparency multiplied by excellence, ethics and eternity -- personified in former Senate President Jovito R. Salonga.
sub_topics: He thanked Phi Kappa Phi president Dr. Sonia Yuson de Leon, recalled meeting her and her husband in the late Fifties as UP scholars and Student Catholic Action leaders, and noted this was his second appearance before the society after its 1994 Diamond Year symposium, where he was 'roasted' by the intellectual elite.

He read Time magazine's choice of Einstein over Roosevelt and Gandhi as Person of the Century as a triumph of pure excellence, crediting Einstein's probe of the cosmos and the atom -- and light quanta behind the semiconductor and microchip -- with founding the information age.

He illustrated the e-society personally: visiting four of his five children in New York over Christmas 1999, he read the Inquirer, Star and Bulletin online at noon New York time, hours before Manila readers, once quoting headlines to a friend by phone at 4:00 a.m. Manila time.

He described the Coronado Resort at DisneyWorld, where a single plastic card gave access to meals, shops, exhibition halls, studio rides, motorboats and quadcycles in an entertainment city larger than Makati, and his 2000 tour of Turkey, where his Manila mobile phone worked across a 2,000-kilometer bus route.

He contrasted the obsolete method of researching volumes of encyclopedias with Encarta, a single-ounce CD-ROM holding 26,000 topics and nine million words for under $100, itself destined to be phased out by broadband fiber optics.

He noted that while the world advanced, the Philippines remained mired in poverty, rebellion, corruption and criminality, and only partly agreed with the conference theme: excellence should not be confined to government, and in any case excellence is not enough.
Defining excellence from Merriam-Webster as virtue or perfection, he argued that although gifts differ it is everyone's responsibility to develop to the maximum whatever natural gift the Lord gave.

He related his son's long quest for excellence -- management engineering at Ateneo, a summa cum laude music degree at UP, graduate piano in Munich, then Stanford master's degrees and a Ph.D. in Engineering Economic Systems with the Centennial Award -- and his own worry that seventeen years of study delayed a career and family.

He set that against his own path -- two years of preparatory law, four of legal studies, then a lowly associate's post, teaching and business, until at 36 he had a law firm, five children, a house and his first Mercedes Benz, inching up to a Supreme Court seat -- and concluded that both routes reach excellence, asking the audience which is better.

He insisted on general excellence in the humanities alongside career specialization, invoking the race between education and catastrophe and quoting Judge Learned Hand's ideal magistrate acquainted with Acton, Thucydides, Homer, Dante, Machiavelli, Plato and Kant.

On ethics, he grounded professional canons in character ethic and sharply distinguished them from image-building tactics -- ghost-written speeches, alms from ill-gotten money, false war heroes, model spouses with several lovers -- calling such duplicity fundamentally flawed and, in the language of the young, 'plastic.'

He repeated that changing society requires a change in men rather than a change of men, dismissed motivational seminars and quick fixes as Band Aid and aspirin, and quoted Emerson that what you are shouts so loudly that your words cannot be heard.

On eternity he disclosed his poor and secular upbringing -- selling newspapers, shining shoes, peddling textbooks, unable to afford the 15-centavo bus fare to UP -- and that his real introduction to God came only some fifteen years earlier.

He argued that spiritual laws operate like civil, criminal and physical laws: transgressing the Ten Commandments or the Beatitudes brings damnation, while salvation comes by repentance, restitution and reformation.

Turning to the conference's other theme, he agreed that public officials must add transparency, citing the Constitution's policy of full public disclosure, the right to information, the command that public officers be accountable, and the sanctions of the Ethical Standards Law (RA 6713).

In his epilogue he coined the Einstein-flavored equation GG=TE3 and proposed a Search for Ideal Public Servants, nominating Jovito R. Salonga -- bar topnotcher, Harvard and Yale graduate, thrice number-one senator, who dissolved rather than merely left his law office after EDSA, gave free legal service, and authored the Ethical Standards Law -- his professor, dean and guru across four decades and different faiths, closing with Longfellow's 'Psalm of Life.'

notable_anecdotes: From New York over Christmas 1999 he read the Manila dailies online hours before Philippine readers, and once phoned a friend at 4:00 a.m. Manila time who was startled that he could quote that day's headlines verbatim.

At DisneyWorld's Coronado Resort the family was each given a small plastic card that unlocked meals, shops, exhibition halls, studio rides, motorboats and quadcycles across an entertainment city larger than Makati.
Touring Turkey for two weeks in 2000, he was amazed that his Manila-issued mobile phone let him call and text anywhere along a bus tour of more than 2,000 kilometers.

He confessed worrying that his only son, after seventeen years of study and three degrees beyond his bachelor's, would at 36 still be single and penniless -- fears that vanished when Stanford offers poured in and his son entered Bear Stearns as a vice president.

He recalled his own poverty: selling newspapers, shining shoes and peddling textbooks to classmates, and being unable to study at UP because his father could not afford the 15-centavo bus fare from their rented apartment in Sampaloc.
He recalled being 'roasted' by the intellectual elite at Phi Kappa Phi's 1994 Diamond Year symposium, which made him sweat and blush, and returning ready for their fire and coal.

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 5 of 'Transparency, Unanimity & Diversity' reproduced CJP's address to a Phi Kappa Phi and Civil Service Commission round table on 'Excellence in Government Service,' which he only partly endorsed, arguing that excellence should not be confined to government and, more importantly, that excellence is not enough. Opening with Time magazine's choice of Einstein over Roosevelt and Gandhi as Person of the Century, he credited Einstein's work on light quanta and the microchip with founding the information age, then illustrated that age experientially: from New York over Christmas 1999 he read Manila's dailies online hours before their printed copies reached readers; a single plastic card unlocked all of DisneyWorld's Coronado Resort; his Manila mobile phone worked across 2,000 kilometers of Turkey; and Encarta, a single-ounce CD-ROM, had rendered shelves of encyclopedias obsolete. Against this he set a country still mired in poverty, rebellion, corruption and criminality. He then took up his three Es. On excellence he argued that each person must develop to the maximum whatever gift the Lord gave, illustrating with the contrasting careers of his son -- seventeen years of study from Ateneo to a Stanford doctorate, then straight into a Bear Stearns vice presidency -- and his own short schooling followed by a climb from lowly associate to Supreme Court justice, and quoted Learned Hand on the magistrate who must know Thucydides and Kant as well as the law. On ethics he grounded professional canons in character ethic, distinguished them sharply from image-building tactics and spin, and repeated that society needs a change in men rather than a change of men. On eternity he disclosed his poor, secular upbringing and his late introduction to God, and argued that spiritual laws carry consequences just as civil and physical laws do, with salvation by repentance, restitution and reformation. He added transparency for public officials, citing the Constitution's disclosure and accountability commands and RA 6713, and closed with the equation GG=TE3, nominating Jovito R. Salonga as its personification.
